zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical review aid: NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Consulted after independent scan reading; the transcription and review notes are this reviewer's work, not a reproduction of the index.

lines.note: Racurui denotes falling tears, matching the Japanese paraphrase. The initial is R rather than OCR C; this headword also identifies the preceding page's catchword.
Completes ca-/yem dos olhos, tears falling from the eyes. The initial has the descending stroke of y, not the OCR v; the historical cayem is retained rather than modernized to caem.

runs.text: Sobejos como de comer, &c. que fi-

lines.note: Racusacu names leftovers, particularly food scraps. The following rows explain what remains after dividing or carving something.

runs.text: cão dalgũa couſa que ſe parte, ou trincha depo-

lines.note: Completes ficão and describes leftovers from something cut or carved. The printed division depo-/is and the tilde carrier in dalgũa are preserved.
Completes depois and specifies what remains after the best has been taken. The Japanese example begins offering these leftovers to someone.

runs.text: Conuidar a alguem com eſtes ſobejos.

lines.note: Completes furumǒ, entertaining or treating someone with the leftovers. The long-o mark is a caron and the Portuguese supplies the hospitality sense.

runs.text: Racuxa. Tanoximu mono. i, Racuuo ſuru

lines.note: Racuxa is a person who enjoys pleasure, with two synonymous Japanese descriptions. Its initial R corrects OCR B; the second description continues below.
Mono completes the person-denoting phrase. The Portuguese characterizes someone devoted to delights and pleasures, retaining its printed à.
Racuxo first denotes the place to which someone has fled or taken refuge. The Japanese falling-place paraphrase is interpreted through the following Portuguese explanation.
Completes the refuge definition and gives a Japanese question about the fugitive's whereabouts. The question is a standalone example, not an embedded Portuguese typeface-toggle term.

runs.text: Onde estarà o q̃ ſe acolheo, & fugio? ¶ Item,

lines.note: Translates the question as asking where the person who fled may be. The paragraph sign introduces an additional figurative sense below.

runs.text: per met. Falta, ou erro em que hum cahio.

lines.note: The figurative sense is a fault or error into which someone has fallen. Enlargement distinguishes the shorter, cross-stroked t in Falta from the preceding l; this corrects the provisional Falla rather than modernizing the wording.
A separate Racuxo concerns a written paper or placard. Its explanation continues with a publicly posted lampoon, rather than the refuge sense above.

runs.text: paſquim que ſe poem em publico contra alguem.

lines.note: Specifies a pasquim displayed publicly against someone. The printed spelling poem is retained without supplying a modern accent.
The Japanese example means putting up the lampoon. Portuguese Por is the infinitive for placing here, not the preposition in an unrelated phrase.
Racuyǒ is glossed as the court or principal city. The repeated Miyaco miyaco is printed as the Japanese explanation and is not removed as duplication.
Completes the description of the court as the kingdom's principal city. This is the capital-city sense of Racuyǒ.

runs.text: Folha caida, ou o cair das

lines.note: This distinct Racuyô denotes a fallen leaf or the falling of leaves. Its final circumflex differs from the preceding entry's caron; cair das has a real word boundary.
Completes the falling-of-leaves definition. The single-word line remains separate from the new thunder entry.

Rai is thunder or a thunderbolt, with two Japanese synonyms. The damaged a and medial m are restored from surviving strokes and the coherent forms; the headword is upright throughout, not partly italic.
The example describes a thunderbolt falling upon something. Raiga, with a damaged a, replaces OCR Reniga; the attached ga is the subject particle.
Completes the object of the lightning strike as some thing. The faint interior vowel is read as u in couſa rather than the OCR's a.
A separate Rai is equated with Rei and means reverence or worship. The example marker Vt is italic with the Portuguese apparatus.
Rai suru means to worship or revere. The repeated stem's a is abraded but recoverable; the printed joining Raiſuru is preserved.
Raibin denotes an incoming messenger or opportunity for communication. The explanatory tayori is one word; the apparent internal gap comes from abrasion, not a separate ta.

runs.text: ou portador que ha de vir.

lines.note: Adds a bearer who is to come, completing the messenger definition. The final S. is an upright written-register label.
Raibiǒ is explained by the historical Japanese name for leprosy. The Portuguese confirms the disease identification; the historical wording is retained as source text.

Raibon is a grinding bowl or mortar. The initial syllables read Rai-, not OCR Rui-. Enlargement confirms the small grave over e in manèira; it is preserved as a local printed accent rather than normalized away.

runs.text: largo de barro em q̃ moẽ Miſo, moſtarda, &c.

lines.note: Describes a broad earthenware bowl for grinding miso, mustard, and similar substances. Miſo is Japanese embedded in the Portuguese explanation and is marked for optional whole-word typeface review.
This Raica denotes an honoured person's going or coming in a conveyance. The gloss continues with the litter or sedan-chair description below.
Completes the explanation as an honoured person travelling in a litter. The phrase remains Portuguese, not a separate Japanese example.
A separate Raica means the coming summer. The explanatory initial is a damaged Q, not G; natçu provides the seasonal meaning.

runs.text: O vir ao reino de Iapão.

lines.note: Raichô denotes coming to Japan. The headword bears a circumflex; the final S. is upright, while Portuguese Iapão stays in the italic gloss.
Raicǒ is explained as coming to meet, introducing a religious appearance or reception. The two carons are preserved independently of modern romanization.

runs.text: Amida, ou outro Fotoque a receber as almas. Po

lines.note: Specifies Amida or another Buddha appearing to receive souls. Amida and Fotoque are Japanese names within Portuguese explanation; Po starts Pode without a secure edge hyphen.

runs.text: de ſe accõmodar eſta palaura a Deos, & Anjos.

lines.note: Completes Pode and says the expression can be adapted to God and angels. This is the compilers' proposed Christian usage, not an editorial replacement of the Buddhist sense.
Raiden combines thunder and lightning in the Japanese explanation. The scan supports Caminari and Portuguese Trouão, rather than OCR Camimari and Tronão.
Completes the storm terminology and begins the Japanese example Raidenga suru. The verb is physically divided ſu-/ru.
Completes suru and translates the occurrence of thunder and lightning. Auer retains the historical spelling rather than modern haver.
Raifai denotes worship or paying reverence. Its medial f belongs to the historical Japanese spelling and is not replaced by long s.

runs.text: Hum como estrado, ou aßento redon-

lines.note: Raifan is described as a platform or round seat used for worship. The shape adjective is divided redon-/do at the physical boundary.

runs.text: do hum pouco alto, ſobre que fazem adoração

lines.note: Completes round and says the seat is slightly raised, with worship performed upon it. The religious setting is completed on the next row.
Locates the act of worship before the Buddha. Fotoque is a Japanese term embedded in the Portuguese sentence, not a standalone headword here.
Raifaru means the coming spring; the apparatus recommends Raixun as the better form. The italic Meliùs and its grave are retained, while the recommended headword begins R, not B.
Translates the coming spring. The worn interior vowel supports primauera; the OCR's primau ra represented abrasion, not two printed words.
Raifǔ denotes an approaching wind. The scan supplies the missing vowel and caron in the headword; the Portuguese vẽ-/tando retains abbreviation and physical division.
Completes the wind-blowing description. The short final row is body text followed by an upright register label, not bottom furniture.
The alternative forms denote the coming month. The scan reads Qitaru tçuqi, correcting the OCR's changed vowel and extra j; the final t in the headwords is preserved.
Completes month or moon to come, using the lunar sense of tçuqi. The tilde remains over u in lũa.
Raiguen means appearing or coming into manifestation. The Japanese explanation combines coming with becoming visible; the Portuguese alternative continues below.
Completes manifesting oneself. The final upright S. marks written usage rather than forming part of the verb.
Repeats the coming-month meaning under the alternative headword. The joined Qitaru and abbreviated vẽ are visible; the latter begins v rather than OCR u.
Raigui denotes the arrival of a noble person. The explanatory Von ide retains its printed space rather than being forced to match the joined form elsewhere.
Adds high-ranking as an alternative description of the arriving person. This is a continuation of the status qualification, not physical height in a separate entry.

runs.text: Portador, ou ocaſião de recado que

lines.note: Rai-in concerns an incoming bearer or opportunity for a message. The headword's internal hyphen is printed; recado corrects the OCR's recedo.
Completes the description of a message opportunity that comes. The upright S. is the written-register label.
Raiji denotes a person with leprosy and introduces a historical saying about drawing one's fellows. The sentence-end dot after fiqu is visible at the right edge.

runs.text: O leproſo acompanha o leproſo. i, Ca-

lines.note: Xix. is an upright source label. The Portuguese translates the saying and begins its general explanation: each person seeks someone like himself; the historical disease wording is preserved as a quotation.
Completes Cada hum, each person seeking his like. The first letter of hum is h, not the OCR's b; the final S. remains outside the italic explanation.
Raijin is another historical term for a person with leprosy. The scan supports Rai-, not OCR Roai-; Lazaro is part of the Portuguese gloss.
Raijit denotes the coming day. Qitaru is continuous, and the headword's checked final t is not expanded into another syllable.
Raimei is the sounding of thunder, matching the Japanese verb naru. The final S. is a separate upright register label.
Rainen means the coming year. The apparent OCR space after Q is not a Japanese word division, and the printed doubled n in Anno is retained.
Rainhǔ denotes coming and entering. The native scan shows h followed by caroned u, not the OCR's hiǒ; the Japanese explanation confirms the entry's sense without replacing its spelling.
Rainǒ concerns incoming receipts or yield, paraphrased as an arriving payment. The headword's caron and the long s in voſame are retained.
Completes the gloss as forthcoming yield or produce. In this context nouidade belongs with rendimento, rather than necessarily meaning news.

runs.text: Hũ dos cinco liuros que enſinão policia,

lines.note: Raiqi names one of five books said to teach orderly conduct. The gloss's policia is interpreted through the following reference to courtesies, not as a modern police institution.
Adds courtesies and related conduct to the book's subject matter. This short continuation completes the description of Raiqi.
Raiqua is literally the fire of thunder, glossed as a thunderbolt or lightning. Relampago is divided at the physical line ending.
Completes lightning that falls downwards. The printed caye and two-word em baixo are retained without modernizing.
Raiquǒ is the light of thunder, glossed directly as lightning. The headword's long-o mark is a caron.

runs.text: Principio, ou origem donde ſe vai de

lines.note: Raireqi concerns the beginning or origin from which something is traced. The edge has de without a secure hyphen before duzindo on the next row.

Completes deduzindo and describes derivation or a course of development. The u and its abbreviation mark in algũa are abraded; the chosen marked reading remains uncertain. The small oblique mark in Mõ- is read as a tilde rather than the provisional caron, consistent with the religious-school expression completed below, but its exact shape is a nonblocking caveat.

Completes Mõpano raireqiuo xiru, knowing the origin or history of a religious school. The object particle uo remains attached to raireqi; the preceding row retains the abbreviation mark instead of expanding it into n.
Adds descent or propagation of a religion to the account of its origin. The historical spelling decendencia is preserved without supplying modern s.
Completes religion or sect. It finishes the object of the preceding historical example, not a separate entry.
Rairin denotes the arrival of a noble person. The scan shows initial R, joined Qitari, and the Portuguese division Vin-/da, not OCR Fairin or Vir-.
Completes Vinda de peßoa nobre. The final upright S. qualifies the usage of the arrival term.
Raisǒ denotes leprosy, followed by an example meaning to suffer from it. All three caron-marked o vowels and the short s in both occurrences of the disease name are retained as printed.
Translates the preceding example as being ill with leprosy. It is the infinitival explanation of vazzurǒ, not a new headword.
Raitei denotes thunder and lightning. The capital I of Inabicari is visibly printed and is not harmonized with the lowercase synonym elsewhere.
Completes thunder and lightning. The upright S. marks the written register of the headword.
Raitô means the coming winter. The scan shows a circumflex rather than the OCR caron; the Portuguese retains initial capital I and abbreviated vẽ.
Rai v combines thunder and rain. The scan has a visible gap before v, which is preserved instead of joining Raiv. The tilde is carried by o in Trouaõ, and the final S. is upright.
Raiuǒ denotes going and coming, directly matched by the Portuguese pair. The comma between the Japanese verbs is retained.
Raixa is referred to Raijin, another historical term for a person with leprosy. The synonym is not marked as an embedded Portuguese font-toggle term.
Raixe concerns the next world or future existence. The synonym begins G in the scan, not OCR C; mundo is divided at the right edge.
Completes the other world and adds the future world as a paraphrase. It continues the religious-temporal sense of Raixe.
Raixei is the sound of thunder, explicitly paraphrased in Japanese. The Portuguese word trouaõ is divided across this and the next row.
Completes trouaõ and gives an example of thunder being clamorous to the ears. The final character is the Portuguese article O, not OCR Q, and belongs to the italic translation.

runs.text: ſom do trouaõ atroa os ouuidos.

lines.note: Translates the thunder sound as deafening or overwhelming the ears. The o-carried tilde in trouaõ and the historical ouuidos are preserved.

runs.text: Papel q̃ ſe poem por reuerencia limpo,

lines.note: Describes clean paper supplied as a mark of respect. The headword visibly prints Ranxi, although the continuation on f413 uses Raixiuo; this apparent printed anomaly is retained rather than silently changed to Raixi.

runs.text: como hũa folha de papel junto com a carta eſ-

lines.note: Explains a clean sheet accompanying the written letter. The word escrita is divided eſ-/crita; the row remains part of the same paper-etiquette entry.

runs.text: crita. ¶ Item, permet. Parte da carta que

lines.note: Completes escrita and adds a figurative sense: the part of a letter left blank. Enlargement recovers the full apparatus and carta from the garbled OCR; the sentence continues on f413, anticipated by the catchword ſe.
